title: "Teaching Physical AI"
subtitle: "Instructor guide · MLSysBook Volume IV · Draft"
---

## Course scope

Physical AI systems act on the world through sensors and actuators. A learned
policy proposes an action, while an independent governor checks whether to permit
it. Students must measure the resulting motion and use a new observation to
decide what happens next. The course therefore assesses the complete physical
loop, including the command checks that limit the policy's authority.

The [Physical AI course overview](https://mlsysbook.ai/courses/physical-ai/)
connects this material to [MLSysBook Volume IV](https://harvard-edge.github.io/cs249r_book_dev/vol4/).
The [ETH Zurich spring 2027 offering](https://mlsysbook.ai/courses/physical-ai/eth-spring-2027/)
provides a draft seminar and studio plan. Its
[syllabus](https://mlsysbook.ai/courses/physical-ai/eth-spring-2027/syllabus.html)
is the source for that offering's schedule, grading, and policies. Other
institutions can adapt the plan to their term and available equipment.

## Teaching format and preparation

The reference plan pairs a systems seminar with a supervised hardware studio.
Students read the assigned chapter, predict the outcome of an experiment, and
compare their prediction with measurements from the station. Teams maintain a
shared notebook so that later experiments can use earlier calibration results,
baselines, and failure records.

Students need Python, introductory machine learning, basic linear algebra and
probability, and first-year Newtonian physics. The teaching team provides the
baseline firmware and supports its extension. Students do not need prior
experience with the proposed arm or microcontroller, but staff must be able to
commission and maintain both before teaching begins.

## Station and compute requirements

The proposed reference station combines a Seeed SO-101 arm, an overhead camera,
and an Arduino UNO Q. The UNO Q's Linux processor runs the policy, and its STM32
microcontroller governs the motor command path. The
[station reference](https://harvard-edge.github.io/cs249r_book_dev/labs/vol4/labs/station-reference.html)
defines the hardware and the measurements required at the command boundaries.

The station remains a proposal until staff demonstrate the complete command
path on the assembled hardware. Connecting a host directly to the arm's motor
bus does not by itself give the microcontroller authority over each command.
Staff must qualify that interface, the independent motor cutoff, the operating
limits, and restart behavior before student use.

Training and fine-tuning require workstation compute; deployment is evaluated on
the edge station. The course has not yet fixed a minimum training configuration
or a required policy. Staff must select the model, dataset, simulator, and export
path, then measure their memory use and execution time on the actual equipment.
The introductory curriculum's optional-hardware and no-GPU assumptions do not
apply to this studio.

## Preparation before enrollment

Staff should complete a trial of the student workflow before setting enrollment
or purchasing a class set. The trial must establish that the policy proposes an
action, the governor permits or refuses it, the actuator responds within the
measured limits, and a fresh observation records the result. It must also test
refusal, stale commands, interruption, and recovery under the declared fault
conditions.

A successful trial needs reproducible instructions and a measured session time.
The teaching team can then determine station capacity, supervision, spare parts,
and bookable bench time. Starter firmware, a baseline controller, sample traces,
and a tested model checkpoint should be available before the first lab.

The [hardware feasibility plan](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/blob/dev/labs/vol4/staff/feasibility-plan.md)
and [first-offering teaching plan](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/blob/dev/instructors/vol4/first-offering-plan.md)
contain the detailed staff preparation work. These are planning documents;
they do not establish that the proposed station has passed qualification.

## Assessment and adaptation

The labs build one system through physical measurement, simulation, learned
control, adaptation, disturbance tests, and governor checks. The
[lab sequence](https://mlsysbook.ai/courses/physical-ai/eth-spring-2027/#labs)
and [competency card](https://harvard-edge.github.io/cs249r_book_dev/labs/vol4/curriculum/student-competencies.html)
connect those experiments to observable student skills.

Assessment should distinguish model quality from physical task outcomes. A
policy can score well offline and still fail to recover from a disturbance or
issue a command outside the permitted limits. Teams therefore submit raw traces,
baseline comparisons, and fault evidence as part of a Physical Release Dossier.
Each student defends the release decision individually. A well-supported decision
to withhold release can earn full marks.

An adapted course can change the task, term length, and hardware after staff
qualify the resulting station. The assessed system must still separate learned
proposals from command permission and demonstrate physical outcomes with
measurements. General guidance on [pedagogy](../pedagogy.qmd),
[assessment](../assessment.qmd), and [teaching-assistant preparation](../ta-guide.qmd)
is available in the Instructor Hub.
